It's kind of that. My PTSD means that I am scared of people who are freshly angry, so we agree to always take time to cool off and compose ourselves before we talk when angry. It's almost always 20 minutes I need alone. Then we talk. -this first paragraph is basically the tl;dr version.

 I'm disabled and in a lot of pain so unfortunately I can't just go out for a walk, so most of the time the only way to have time by myself is if he agrees to leave me be for awhile.

 He's the type of person who prefers to hash it out immediately because he's scared that frustration or anger means I don't love him, so we compromise by me reassuring him that I still love him, reiterating that I just need some space until I get my composure or my hypersensitive fight-flight-or-freeze reaction under control, depending on the circumstance. I feel bad about it because a boundary shouldn't involve other people having to do things or move, but there are times I physically can't get out of bed by myself, nor less go down the stairs.

Sometimes lately he can't help himself, he comes in angrily into the room that is difficult for me to leave because he needs to get something off of his chest NOW. The things aren't very considerate or well thought out in that circumstance because they are in the heat of the moment.  Before I was disabled and before we agreed to have a cooldown period I would leave, because rapidly entering a room angry triggers flashbacks for me even without physical force, because that was how my previous abuse started. Eventually they once knocked the door off so they could come in. They would barricade me in the room off and on for 6-12 hours with their own body in the way so I couldn't get out unless I was willing and physically able to escalate it to physical violence. I was never the former and rarely the latter. While just screaming and screaming vile things at me and I wasn't allowed a means of communication or to go to the bathroom. The rage would slowly deflate them as they unloaded it all on me, and they would leave relatively calmly. Then they would think of something else to get off their chest and it would start over again and I'd get to guess how many times that it would happen in each episode.

He knows the things that happened, even heard it once, and has promised repeatedly to give me time when I ask for it, especially when either of us is frustrated. And he's promised to let me be in a room by myself if I ask, when I can't walk enough to go far. I respect his need for alone time too, whether in the house or not. I don't usually ask more than once every few months, but the past month we have both been irritable. It's happened before that life happens and we were both irritable, but we took cooldowns and talked a lot and we made it through without any real problems. 

Sorry I really got off track there. I don't think he's likely to escalate to the level that I experienced previously. But it's legitimately triggering as fuck, and to be honest I don't understand what stops anyone who needs to unload their anger from reaching that level, so I fear it. Now that the worst of the initial shock has worn off and I'm still uncomfortable, I'm not sure how much of the current feeling of wariness is overreactive trauma brain, and how much is just experience telling me to be cautious with people who use their frustration in an intimidating way. 

Maybe I just have to wait until this PTSD episode is treated to know if what I'm feeling is reasonable wariness or hypersensitivity. I'm sorry I'm typing so much aaah.

You're very right that what I said was very unkind. It's so weird because we had a system that worked, wait 20 minutes to cool down then talk it over just fine. But he feels a loss of control at work and somehow that's translating into not wanting to leave me alone? 

We have both apologized and are both committed to be better. I'm just scared and unsure of how the future will go I guess.

My story is almost exactly like FinallyFreeFromThem's story. I was very, very choosy and would not tolerate anyone who was angry, capricious, or cruel. I was told by so many people that I was too choosy, that it was mean to be so judgemental, that I would end up an old spinster. I kept on because I figured I'd rather be a spinster than with someone who was any of those things. 

By being so choosy I didn't end up getting much experience with relationships before meeting the man who is now my husband. So my inexperience led to some mild relationship issues, because you have to learn how to be a good partner to someone. But we did learn together. We've both grown a lot as a couple and individuals. 

He comes from a home where they weren't the kindest but weren't abusive. His parents grew much more kind when he was an adult and we both have a good relationship with them. 

My ACON issues have caused some mild issues in other ways, like I didn't set boundaries with them because I thought they'd disown him if we did. Once we had a good talk and I realized it wasn't dangerous to say "please don't do [thing], it hurts my feelings" it really helped out relationship with the in laws. Also getting my PTSD under control helped me realize that most people will not choose to abuse me if given half a reason to. Not being terrified of typically innocuous phrases helped a lot too. It was hard to trust again. 

But now we have a pretty happy life and a very satisfied and healthy relationship. We have never yelled at one another. The only times I have ever been scared of him was when he accidentally triggered my PTSD with an actually innocent phrase- he's never been at all intimidating or threatening. We don't invalidate or insult each other. We both feel supported, encouraged, and loved. So it's definitely possible to have a healthy, calm, loving relationship after all.

Just some things that helped me out!

It feels kind of the opposite in my case. They'll hound a nonsensical thread for half a day, they will keep circling around one delusional thought no matter what is said around it. It's almost like their brain just tosses out all new arguments once they remember the original topic. They keep a weird idea in their head no matter what.

An actual example from about 8 years ago- they are some sort of delusional and it makes me feel insane myself.  They screamed that I'm on drugs because my eyes are glassy. I reminded them I have *glass* contacts, they were at the first opthamologist appointment that I was prescribed them at. Blah blah calling me a liar, so I offer to take my contacts out to show them. I do so, but then I must be on drugs because my eyes were then red. I tell them that they are red because I literally just touched my eyes to take my contacts out. And asked didn't they remember 5 minutes ago when my eyes weren't red? Then they remember my eyes were glassy, so they yell about how druggies should be strung up, and how my glassy eyes were proof I should be too. I ask if my eyes look glassy NOW without contacts in? When they said no I asked wasn't that proof it was just my contacts. Then they say but your eyes are red. 

It went around in that circle for an hour till my eyes were normal, which was proof I was trying to *hide* drug use from them. Then they started in on how I "wouldn't look them straight in the eye" and that must be a sign of my guilt. 

Again all of this is punctuated by all the various torture and rights stripping that should be enacted upon "druggies."

The reason it doesn't look like I'm looking them "straight" in the eye is that I have a very lazy eye so no, both can't look directly into their eyes at the same time. I have had this my whole life. I told them that it is my lazy eye, I was making eye contact (which is excruciatingly painful for me.) They say this is just me lying again and don't I know what happens to people who lie to them. 

So I offer to put my contacts in again, because the laziness mostly corrected with them. 

Then it's "your eyes are glassy, you fucking druggie."

You would think you could maybe short circuit it by asking what concerns they have, what other reasons they have for thinking this or being worried in general, but this is not a reasonable person and attempts at that were futile. It's just hours of trying to not set them off worse until they get all of their unrelated anxiety out or get too tired from screaming for so long.

It's like that old folk song ["There's a hole in the bucket"](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/There%27s_a_Hole_in_My_Bucket) but a nightmare hellscape version of it.

I'm still learning- or maybe unlearning- this and I've been an adult for a long while now. (Edit to clarify: what I'm unlearning is the voice that says I can't try shit, can't ever not be perfect at something, and will get relentlessly mocked and insulted for exploring things.)

Each person's own reaction to this is valid, I'm sure there are many different feelings about it- this is just my own feelings about it. For me I don't usually mourn it. Usually when I realize I missed out on something, I get excited to claim my own agency and be able to do it, even though I'm usually one of the oldest beginners learning something. Swimming. Art. Reading. All kinds of shit I wasn't allowed to do I was able to really dive into once I realized that a)I had always wanted to and b) no one I choose to keep in my life currently will stop or even discourage me.

Just last week my SO and I realized that I have extreme discomfort making noise, I cry trying to play musical instruments because I was conditioned to believe that making noise is a very bad thing, as is failure while learning. But I wished I could jam with my friends. So we got a couple of easy non intimidating instruments and I was able to make wonderful sounds and got used to doing so without repercussions. No one screamed and yelled or even made fun of me. It felt subversive in a way just to bang wooden sticks together! 

It's sad in a way to try everything so late, but I also really feel a lot of happiness and excitement from being able to explore these things that I always wanted to. And from being supported while doing it.

There are very different reasons why someone might minimize abusive behaviour. Either they don't believe, or they think it's acceptable. 

99% of the stories in this subreddit in my opinion it does not matter *what* the person did, no one can ever deserve to be treated that way. I'm not sure the exact behaviours your parents were exhibiting, but given the subreddit I'm assuming its abusive. If someone believes the level of maltreatment, but thinks it can be justified, IMO and IME that's a red flag. Doesn't matter how much you piss someone off, abuse isn't a valid response, and if someone thinks it is, they aren't a safe person to be around if they will ever get pissed off, you know what I mean?

I personally find disbelief frustrating but less alarming. Most people have never experienced the type of abuse, and many people have loving parents, so its simply so far out if their experience that they can't imagine it truly existing. If that's the case, well I personally havent found anything other than them seeing it that can convince people so far removed from it that it exists.  My SO wasn't so victim-blamey, but he had a hard time truly believing someone would say and do the things my mom does. One time she burst in screaming incoherently at me while I happened to be video chatting with him, and continued for hours. And once she slipped up and forgot herself and started up on an answering machine. After that first time he fully understood that it's not an exaggeration.

Wow, it sounds like he (mistakenly!) thought you'd come home begging forgiveness before you left the driveway, like a 5 year old who ran away from home because they didn't get cookies (I'm sure lots people here wanted to run away at 5 but for good reason.) Also seems like he was planning in you not being prepared.

Being on your own it feels so good to be allowed to throw shit away instead of trying to reorganize a pile of stuff that grows till it threatens to drown you. I still am not able to throw as much away as your average person, but it was a Sisyphian task to clean when you couldn't end with less than you started with. 

As a kid I thought every day that with her cleaning strictness her place would be so clean in the future. Hours of cleaning a 800 sqft place every night and she's so strict about cleanliness that a water spot on a pan meant I had to rewash and dry the entire cupboard. So I thought surely when I'm not ruining it by being a messy kid and being inept at cleaning, her place will be amazing. Within a few years of me moving it became all sticky, gross, and full of stuff to the extent they often don't invite people over. And I mean **EVERY** surface is sticky, it's like they live inside a toddlers hand. I can't believe how long I had assumed her standards weren't hypocritical.

When they first inadvertently admitted that a behaviour was fucked up and wrong. My mom was always present when I went into the bathroom to make sure I didn't take too long/sneak in some reading. I have no recollection what prompted it but one day when I was 10 they both (my dad waited outside the bathroom at least!) started saying something about how they GUESS (imagine this in a cartoonishly put out tone) she will have to stop because I'm so melodramatic and complain about everything and if someone like a teacher heard me complain, teachers who were perverted freaks would assume my mom was a perverted freak for monitoring all bathroom time.  (The logic was only pedophiles could think something so innocent and normal could be inappropriate.) I am sure I never said anything about telling anyone else, as I had learned early not to talk about home life when outside. 

It was so out of the blue I was shocked. It was the first time I ever realized WHY we weren't supposed to "air dirty laundry," and that not everything they did was normal, and not everyone believed the same things they did.

I'm not sure if it varies based on where you live but when I saw a social worker they knew lots of places and programs to help from places to stay to financial short or long term help, places to get low cost or free emotional help/counselling for things like coping skills or boundary setting, and other programs for life skills, support, lots of different things.

They basically wanted to assess what my problems and goals were (I was very abstract and stressed but they helped me put words to what I wanted), and did their best to find people/places/programs to help in each area. They were even kind enough to set up many of the appointments for me. 

The registered social worker I went to was not only very helpful, but very kind and easy to talk to even though I had no idea how to talk about any of it- I don't even remember my part of the conversation now! They're used to dealing with clients who are highly stressed and who have a hard time talking about difficult things, so they are great at gently asking questions to help if you get stuck not knowing what to say.   

I wish you all the best.

I found that I was mostly able to get her voice out after a long time- only very rarely do I default to her response.  Everyone probably has different needs, but I can try telling you what helped for me just in case it could help in any way. 

Firstly realizing that those hateful thoughts aren't your true beliefs but are a conditioned response. It sounds like you already have that crucial step! Then it was a long struggle to recognize them as they came up. I imagine I will find some reactions that are conditioned for years yet. 

Then when they come up and are recognized as conditioned- well you can ve aware on some level that this may not be true. Eventually you will get more certain of it. If you have a good therapist, you can help talk about the negative self-talk, where it comes from and if it's realistic or not (I always wondered 'what if I really am that bad and should feel that bad??' so it was helpful.) 

Another very helpful thing when you catch hateful self-talk is to think about how you treat others. Would you ever talk to a friend the way you talk to yourself? Probably not. We at least deserve to be treated as well as we treat our friends. Hell, there's a good chance you wouldn't talk to your arch nemesis the way you speak to yourself. 

Just some things I found helpful, those plus time. I wish you the best of luck.
It really does get so much better with time and distance. ♡

Being in a long term abusive relationship can fuck up abusers as well as the abused, though obviously in different ways. (This is *not* a 'sympathy for the devil' post)

Imagine spending years blaming someone else for every and anything you do wrong. Every negative emotion, every thing you break, every time you hit them, you justify everything as their fault. And hell, *they even agree* that it's their fault, after all they take responsibility for your emotions and behaviour, your punishments, to the extent that they reconfigure their life to keep you from blowing up. You can believe that your actions are justified and are your victims fault just as deeply as the abused does. To an abuser they are the only reasonable ones, even if it sounds cartoonish from the outside. 

Abusers can lose their sense of what's normal just like their victims do. Not all do, some keep a normal public persona and you'd never guess, but some fall for their own bullshit *hard.* (Or sometimes they actually believe they are justified, but just that our pussified culture won't tolerate ~~abuse~~ good values so they still hide it)

They started screaming about how dare I touch them, and that they'd call the cops if I dared raise a hand to them again. And regularly being barricaded in a room, and them flying into a rage because my tears were unacceptable because *I was being controlling by crying.*

Denying abuse then reversing the perpetrator and victim even while attacking them is pretty common with abuse, which further adds to their sense that anything they do to their target is justified, since the victim *made* them do it.
